entry: Condition of having at least three loose, liquid or watery bowel movements a day. The most common cause is an intestinal infection by a virus, bacterium or parasite, known as [[Gastroenteritis]], often acquired from food or water contaminated by feces. Non-infectious causes include [[Lactose|lactose]] intolerance, drug withdrawal and [[Irritable bowel syndrome]]. Diarrhea can result in dehydration from fluid loss. Prevention includes [[Sanitation|sanitation]], clean [[Drinking water|drinking water]], handwashing and breastfeeding, along with [[Rotavirus|rotavirus]] vaccination. Oral rehydration solution, clean water with modest amounts of salts and sugar, is the treatment of choice, and [[Zinc|zinc]] tablets are also recommended. These treatments have been estimated to have saved 50 million children in the past 25 years. About 1.7 to 5 billion cases occur per year, mostly in developing countries, where diarrhea is a common cause of [[Malnutrition|malnutrition]].

Written or audiovisual record of events, with discrete entries arranged by date. Diaries were traditionally handwritten but are now often digital. A personal diary may record a writer's experiences, thoughts and feelings, and someone who keeps one is a diarist. Diaries kept for institutional purposes include government records such as Hansard, business ledgers and military records. Personal diaries are generally intended to remain private. The word journal is sometimes used for diary, but a diary generally has daily entries, whereas journal-writing can be less frequent. The earliest known book resembling a diary is *Diary of Merer*, an ancient Egyptian logbook describing the transport of limestone to [[Giza]]. The Greek *Meditations* of the Roman emperor [[Marcus Aurelius]], written in the second half of the 2nd century AD, already displays many characteristics of a diary. The earliest recorded use of the word for a daily record is in [[Ben Jonson]]'s comedy *Volpone* (1605).

American illustrated children's novel series and media franchise by Jeff Kinney. Its narrator, Greg Heffley, illustrates his daily life in a [[Diary|diary]] that he insists is a journal. The series began as an online version on Funbrain in 2004, and the first printed book was published by Abrams Books in April 2007. As of October 2026, the main series has twenty-one books. Films produced by [[20th Century Studios]] began in 2010, and the later installments are animated. More than 250 million copies had been sold by 2020, making it the fourth best-selling book series of all time.

Population dispersed across multiple regions outside its geographic place of origin. Members typically continue to identify culturally, politically, religiously or emotionally with a homeland. The term comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] word *diaspora*, meaning "dispersion," and was first used of the Jewish exile from Judea following the [[Babylonian captivity]]. It now also covers communities formed by voluntary migration, such as trade or education, and by forced displacement through conquest, persecution, enslavement, famine or war. Examples include Armenians, Africans dispersed through the [[Atlantic slave trade]], overseas Chinese, Palestinians, Syrians and Venezuelans. The oldest continuing diaspora is generally considered the Jewish diaspora, which originated in the first millennium BC. The largest today is the Indian diaspora, numbering 17.5 million worldwide as of 2019.

Usually single-celled alga with a silica cell wall. Diatoms generate about 20 to 50 percent of the oxygen produced on Earth each year and take in over 6.7 billion tonnes of [[Silicon|silicon]] annually. Their shells are a significant component of marine sediment. The silica wall, called a frustule, produces structural coloration and has earned diatoms the names "jewels of the sea" and "living opals." About 12,000 species have been documented. Under adequate nutrients and sunlight, a population doubles approximately every 24 hours. Diatoms are phytoplankton, the most common type of [[Plankton|plankton]]. Fossil evidence suggests they originated during or before the early [[Jurassic]] period. Diatomaceous earth, a deposit of their shells, is used for water filtration and as a mild abrasive.

Benzodiazepine medication that acts as an anxiolytic, sold under the brand name Valium among others. It is used to treat [[Anxiety disorder|anxiety]], seizures, alcohol withdrawal, muscle spasms and [[Insomnia|insomnia]]. It works by increasing the effect of the [[Neurotransmitter|neurotransmitter]] gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA). Common side effects include sleepiness and trouble with coordination, and long-term use can lead to dependence. It is not recommended during [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]] or breastfeeding. It has been one of the most frequently prescribed medications in the world since its launch in 1963.

Small throwable objects with marked sides, used to generate random values. A traditional die is a cube whose six faces are marked with one to six pips (dots), and each value is equally likely when it is rolled. Dice are used in [[Board game|board games]], [[Role-playing game|role-playing games]] and games of chance. Dice have been used since before recorded history. Possibly the oldest known dice were excavated at the Burnt City in south-eastern Iran, dated between 2800 and 2500 BCE, and terracotta dice from [[Mohenjo-daro]] date to 2500–1900 BCE. [[Dominoes]] and playing cards are thought to have originated in China as developments from dice. Loaded dice are designed to favor some results over others, for cheating or entertainment.

Colorless, volatile organochlorine solvent, CH₂Cl₂, also called methylene chloride. It has a sweet, chloroform-like odor and is widely used as a solvent. It was historically used to decaffeinate coffee and tea, though supercritical CO₂ has largely replaced it. Its volatility has led to its use as an aerosol propellant and a blowing agent for polyurethane foams. It is produced by chlorinating methane, and it is classified as a probable human [[Carcinogen|carcinogen]] by agencies including the EPA and IARC.

American politician and businessman, 46th vice president of the United States (2001–2009). A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], he had served as White House chief of staff under [[Gerald Ford]] and as secretary of defense under [[George H. W. Bush]]. As vice president under [[George W. Bush]], he played a central role in the response to the [[September 11 attacks]]. He was an early advocate of invading [[Iraq]], alleging that the government of [[Saddam Hussein]] possessed weapons of mass destruction and had ties to [[Al-Qaeda|al-Qaeda]]. Critics argue that neither allegation was ever substantiated.

American actor, comedian, singer and dancer. He became a household name in the United States as Rob Petrie in the [[CBS]] sitcom The Dick Van Dyke Show (1961–1966), which earned him three Primetime Emmy Awards. He won a Tony Award for his role in *Bye Bye Birdie*, and played the chimney sweep Bert in the Disney musical *Mary Poppins* (1964). He was inducted into the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1993 and received the Kennedy Center Honors in 2020.

American television producer and writer, best known for the [[Law & Order]] franchise. Since the original series premiered in 1990, the franchise has included six police and courtroom dramas and four international spin-offs. Wolf is also co-creator and executive producer of the Chicago and FBI franchises. He began as a staff writer on Hill Street Blues and was a writer and co-producer on Miami Vice. He has won two Emmy Awards and has a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

Political leader possessing absolute power. The title originated in the [[Roman Republic]], where a dictator was a magistrate appointed for emergencies. [[Julius Caesar]] was proclaimed dictator in perpetuity in February 44 BC. In modern usage, the term describes a leader who holds or abuses extraordinary personal power. Dictatorships are often marked by suspended elections and civil liberties, rule by decree, repression of political opponents and a [[Cult of personality|cult of personality]] centered on the leader.

Reference work listing the words of one or more languages, usually in alphabetical order. Entries may include definitions, usage, etymologies, pronunciations and translations. Specialized dictionaries cover the terms of particular fields, and bilingual, synonym and rhyming dictionaries form other types. Prescriptive dictionaries reflect what is seen as correct use of a language, while descriptive ones record actual use. The oldest known dictionaries are bilingual Sumerian–Akkadian wordlists from [[Ebla]], dated to roughly 2300 BCE. The oldest surviving monolingual dictionary is the Chinese *Erya*, dating to about the 3rd century BCE. The first purely English alphabetical dictionary was *A Table Alphabeticall* (1604). [[Samuel Johnson]]'s *A Dictionary of the English Language* (1755) set standards for etymologies and quotations, and [[Noah Webster]]'s *An American Dictionary of the English Language* (1828) adapted the form to American usage.

Ivorian former footballer who played as a striker. He is the all-time top scorer for the Ivory Coast national team, with 65 goals in 105 appearances, and Chelsea's all-time top foreign goalscorer. In the 2012 [[UEFA Champions League]] final, he scored an equalizer in the 88th minute and the winning penalty in the shootout against Bayern Munich. He was named African Footballer of the Year in 2006 and 2009.

American action film directed by John McTiernan. [[Bruce Willis]] stars as New York City detective John McClane, who battles terrorists who seize a [[Los Angeles]] skyscraper during a [[Christmas]] Eve party. Adapted from Roderick Thorp's 1979 novel *Nothing Lasts Forever*, it grossed approximately $140 million after its July 1988 release. [[Alan Rickman]]'s portrayal of the villain Hans Gruber was widely praised. The film is credited with revitalizing the [[Action film|action]] genre through its vulnerable hero, and it spawned a franchise and many imitators. It was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry in 2017.

Metal casting process in which molten metal is forced under high pressure into a mold cavity. The mold is formed by two hardened tool steel dies. Most die castings are made from non-ferrous metals such as [[Zinc|zinc]], [[Copper|copper]], [[Aluminium|aluminum]], [[Magnesium|magnesium]], lead and tin-based alloys. Because the equipment and dies are expensive, the process suits high-volume production, and it produces more castings than any other casting process. Die castings have a very good surface finish and dimensional consistency. The equipment was invented in 1838 to produce movable type for the [[Printing|printing]] industry. In 1885 Ottmar Mergenthaler's Linotype machine cast an entire line of type as a single unit using the process. Zinc is the easiest metal to cast, while magnesium is the easiest to machine.

Coral [[Atoll|atoll]], the largest of the Chagos Archipelago in the central Indian Ocean. It is administered by the United Kingdom as part of the [[British Indian Ocean Territory]] and is claimed by [[Mauritius]]. It hosts Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia, a joint British–American military base, and has no permanent inhabitants. Its inhabitants were removed in 1971. In 2019 the [[International Court of Justice]] advised that the United Kingdom should end its administration of the archipelago. A treaty signed on 22 May 2025 would recognize Mauritian sovereignty over the archipelago, including Diego Garcia, but as of November 2026 it had not entered into force.

Argentine football player and manager. Widely regarded as one of the greatest players of all time, he was an attacking midfielder known for his creativity, vision and dribbling. He was named one of the two winners of the FIFA Player of the Century award in 2000, alongside [[Pelé]]. He captained Argentina to victory at the [[FIFA World Cup|1986 World Cup]], scoring five goals and providing five assists, and won the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. In the quarter-final against England he scored both goals, including the "Hand of God," scored with his hand, and the "Goal of the Century," a solo run. He led [[Naples|Napoli]] to its first two Serie A titles, in 1987 and 1990. He struggled with cocaine addiction during his career and received a 15-month suspension in 1991. As manager, he led Argentina to the quarter-finals of the 2010 World Cup. After his death, Argentina declared three days of national mourning.

Mexican painter and muralist. His large frescoes helped establish the mural movement in Mexican and international art. Between 1922 and 1953 he painted murals in [[Mexico City]], Chapingo and Cuernavaca in Mexico, and in [[San Francisco]], [[Detroit]] and [[New York City]]. A retrospective of his work was held at the [[Museum of Modern Art|Museum of Modern Art]] in 1931. His third wife was [[Frida Kahlo]], with whom he had a volatile relationship that lasted until her death. Rivera was an atheist, and his mural *Dreams of a Sunday in the Alameda*, which showed a sign reading "God does not exist," caused a furor. The Mexican government declared his works *monumentos históricos*. His painting *The Rivals* sold for $9.76 million at a 2018 auction.

Spanish Baroque painter, the leading artist at the court of Philip IV. He began painting in a precise tenebrist style and later developed a freer manner with bold brushwork. He was apprenticed to Francisco Pacheco in [[Seville]], and his earliest works are *bodegones*, kitchen scenes with prominent still lifes. He painted many portraits of the Spanish royal family and of commoners, and his masterpiece is *Las Meninas* (1656). His paintings became a model for 19th-century realist and impressionist painters, and in the 20th century [[Pablo Picasso]] and [[Salvador Dalí]] reinterpreted some of his images. Most of his work entered the Spanish royal collection, and the largest collection is in the [[Museo del Prado|Museo del Prado]] in [[Madrid]].

Electrical insulator that can be polarized by an applied electric field. Unlike a conductor, a dielectric has no loosely bound, free electrons to carry current. In an electric field its charges shift slightly from their equilibrium positions, producing an internal field that reduces the overall field. Dielectric properties govern the storage and dissipation of electric and magnetic energy, and they are important in electronics, optics and solid-state physics. A dielectric is the insulating material between the plates of a [[Capacitor|capacitor]], where polarization increases the capacitor's surface charge. The term was coined by William Whewell at the request of [[Michael Faraday]].

Internal combustion engine that ignites its fuel through the heat of compression. Diesel engines compress only air, or air mixed with recirculated exhaust gas, and injected fuel ignites in the hot air. Power is controlled by the amount of fuel injected rather than by throttling the air, so the air-fuel ratio is usually high. Diesel engines have the highest thermal efficiency of any practical internal or external combustion engine, and low-speed marine engines can reach effective efficiencies of up to 55 percent. Named after German engineer [[Rudolf Diesel]], the engine was first used as a more efficient replacement for [[Steam engine|steam engines]]. Since the 1910s it has powered [[Submarine|submarines]] and ships, and it is used in [[Locomotive|locomotives]], [[Bus|buses]] and [[Truck|trucks]]. Controlling its air pollution is harder than for gasoline engines, so in the United States its use is now largely limited to larger vehicles.

Liquid fuel specifically designed for [[Diesel engine|diesel engines]]. The most common type is a fractional distillate of [[Petroleum|petroleum]], although biodiesel and other alternatives are increasingly developed and adopted. Diesel is a high-volume product of oil refineries. As of 2016, almost all petroleum-based diesel in the United Kingdom, mainland Europe and North America was ultra-low-sulfur diesel (ULSD). Diesel fuel originated in experiments by [[Rudolf Diesel]] for his compression-ignition engine, invented around 1892. It is often used in heavy trucks, but diesel exhaust, especially from older engines, can damage health.

Sum of food consumed by a person or other organism. The word often implies a specific intake of nutrition for health or weight-management reasons. Complete nutrition requires vitamins, minerals, essential amino acids and fatty acids, along with energy from carbohydrate, [[Protein (nutrient)|protein]] and fat. A healthy diet can improve and maintain mental and physical health, and specific diets such as the DASH diet are used to manage chronic conditions. Exclusionary diets avoid certain foods; vegetarian and [[Veganism|vegan]] diets can provide adequate nutrition if they focus on protein, iron, calcium, zinc and [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B12]]. Changing dietary intake can promote weight loss or gain. Obesity rates have increased by almost 10% over the past 10 years.

Manufactured product intended to supplement a person's diet, in the form of a pill, capsule, tablet, powder or liquid. Supplements may provide vitamins, minerals, fiber, fatty acids or [[Amino acid|amino acids]], and multivitamins are the most commonly used type. Some contain substances not confirmed as essential, such as plant [[Pigment|pigments]] or polyphenols. In the United States the supplement industry was valued at $151.9 billion in 2021, and about 60% of American adults use dietary supplements. Under the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994, supplements are regulated as foods rather than drugs. Manufacturers may not claim that a product prevents or treats disease, but may use "structure/function" wording with a disclaimer. Systematic reviews have found limited high-quality evidence of broad preventive benefits, and critics argue that regulation is inconsistent.
